candidates.title: Employees Who Use AI End Up Working Vastly More Time Per Day
candidates.raw_excerpt: The world’s capitalists have been waiting with bated breath for the day AI finally delivers on the tech industry’s longstanding promise to create a tool more efficient than human workers. In the four years since AI first became broadly available as a commercial product, these productivity returns have mostly failed to materialize . Now, there’re signs that the push to automate labor is actually backfiring in ironic fashion, as workers who’ve been forced to adopt AI tools are becoming less efficient as time goes on. A new analysis published by the workplace surveillance company ActivTrak, first covered by Gizmodo , found that white collar workers who use AI put in up to 90 minutes more work each day compared to non-users. To arrive at that blistering number, company analysts looked at anonymized work activity from over 9,100 employees at over 450 companies from the period between April and September. For non-AI users observed over that time, the average active workday was 7.6 hours — compared to between 8.4 and 9.1 hours for heavy AI users. For workers, the findings may add to the body of evidence suggesting that sorting through AI-generated slop takes more time than it would to just do workplace tasks by hand. It could also point to the fact that employers aren’t necessarily using AI to replace jobs wholesale, but as an excuse to demand even more labor per worker regardless of any true efficiency gains. From a management point of view, the findings suggest that heavy AI users are having to spend extra billable time working after hours, while experiencing a higher frequency of interrupted work than light- or non-AI users. As head of ActivTrak’s productivity research division Gabriela Mauch wrote in the company’s press report, AI “may help employees complete tasks faster, but our research shows it contributes to longer workdays, more application switching and shorter focus sessions.” More on AI: There Are Now Growing Signs That AI Is Hurting Employment in the Job Mark

Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life. To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life. Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. candidates.title: Scientists Study Difference Between Men Who Pee Standing Up and Sitting Down
candidates.raw_excerpt: One key debate still swirling around men’s health: is it better to pee standing, or sitting down? It may seem like a silly question, but there is some scientific merit to the question. Previous studies have found that men with prostate issues or urinary complications could be better off sitting, pointing to the possibility that plopping down may help loosen up pelvic floor muscles. Unfortunately, the evidence available is far from conclusive — which is probably what inspired the Colombian Urology Research Group to plow ahead with a new study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics . The research, first flagged by Science Alert , took a look at the “posture adopted during voiding” of 52 male volunteers, 24 of whom stood while the rest sat. Each group went on a 24 hour “washout” break in between tests. During the examination, researchers looked at maximum urine flow rate, as well as the total volume of urine expelled in one go. Despite previous polarizing studies on the topic, this piece of research yielded a dull conclusion: it just doesn’t seem to matter. “In healthy men, voiding posture did not significantly modify the maximum urinary flow rate or voided volume,” the team wrote. The one difference between the two postures, the scientists noted, was in what might be called “acceleration.” “The sitting position was associated with a shorter time to maximum flow,” the scientists wrote, noting that it’s a “small difference that is unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Still, you never know until you try. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006 . NASA launches the Mars Global Surveyor to Mars on a Delta II rocket on Nov. 7, 1996. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions. "The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe. candidates.raw_excerpt: We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life." Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024. NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet. By cooling a cloud of rubidium atoms down to an equivalent temperature of 9.7 picokelvin, less than a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero, the research team achieved a milestone in quantum physics.

But first, they had to overcome a major hurdle: gravity.

On Earth, gravity constantly pulls atoms downward. Scientists can't pin the elusive little particles down. And if you can't hold them, you can't cool them.

So, the team engineered a "super fridge" – an ultracold atom physics facility – and launched it to the China Space Station. In microgravity, atoms float freely – much like the toothpaste you've seen in astronaut videos – allowing scientists to cool them to extremes impossible in terrestrial labs.

Getting the facility there was an engineering feat in itself. The original ground-based system weighed a massive 10 tonnes and came in at 20 cubic meters. The space version was shrunk down to just 500 kilograms.

Inside this compact facility, lasers trap the atoms in an optical net and slow them down using evaporative and non-adiabatic cooling techniques without needing bulky magnets.

This orbital lab up will allow scientists to develop quantum sensors and atomic clocks capable of measuring Earth's gravity in unprecedented detail, powering atom interferometers for next-generation navigation systems, and providing a fresh way to probe dark matter and the early universe.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572 , is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. candidates.title: Delivery Robot Causes Car Accident With Nine Injuries
candidates.raw_excerpt: At least nine bus riders were injured when a wayward delivery robot plowed into oncoming traffic in Estonia. The incident happened in the capital city Tallinn, in the middle of rush-hour traffic. As Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported , a delivery robot operated by the company Starship Technologies blundered into an intersection during a “no walk” signal, bringing it squarely into the path of an oncoming bus. Reacting to the obstacle darting out into the road, the bus driver hit the brakes, sending passengers tumbling. The driver’s quick reaction might have actually spared the robot, as the device reportedly continued on its delivery route after colliding with the front of the bus. “The robot fled, if you can put it that way,” as one Tallinn Transport official told ERR . As the spokesperson put it, the robot’s actions may legally constitute fleeing the scene of a traffic incident, meaning Starship Technologies could very well be on the hook for the incident. “If a participant in a traffic accident leaves the scene without fulfilling the obligations prescribed by law, this may constitute an offense,” the transportation official explained. It wouldn’t the company’s first brush with the law. In Arizona, a 73-year-old woman is suing the company after one of its robots allegedly pushed her to the ground, ramming into her repeatedly as she tried to get up. As for the Estonian situation, Starship’s head of operation Pepe Aaviksoo blamed bright ad boards and traffic lights, which apparently disoriented the robot’s sensors. “There are many lessons to be learned, but exceptional situations do occur,” he said. candidates.raw_excerpt: File photo of a Falcon 9 fueled for launch at pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California. Image: SpaceX. SpaceX will deploy another batch of satellites for a clandestine U.S. Space Force program on a Falcon 9 rocket to launch from California Friday afternoon. Liftoff from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base is scheduled for 4:48 p.m. PST (7:48 p.m. EST / 0048 UTC). The rocket will take a south-easterly trajectory on departure from the central California coast. The flight was originally scheduled for Nov. 1 but was delayed repeatedly, first due to delays of the Starlink 15-18 launch, and then for reasons that were not disclosed. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 30 minutes prior to launch. The mission is designated USSF-432 but is also identified as R-4 in public documents. This series of ‘R’ missions began Aug. 16 with USSF-366. More launches in the sequence followed with USSF-153 (R-2) on Sept. 10 and USSF-385 (R3) on Sept. 26. Each R launch has placed 23 satellites in orbit, according to orbital catalog entries. They are thought to be based on SpaceX’s Starshield platform, the government version of the Starlink satellite. According to Jonathan McDowell, the respected tracker of space launches, the R satellites are part of the U.S. Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting program. Officially, the Space Force has declined to provide any information about the missions. The Falcon 9 first stage booster, B1095, is making its eighth flight and is scheduled to land on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You,’ which will be stationed in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Baja California, Mexico.

The companies called the agreement “non-competitive.” Firefly will retain full ownership of its engine intellectual property. Under the terms of the license agreement, AST SpaceMobile will pay approximately $400 million in cash up front and 10 to 14 million shares. It will then pay $250 million for the delivery of engines for its first three rocket launches and $250 million over a three-year period for engineering support services. Launch access has stymied deployment of AST SpaceMobile’s direct-to-device constellation. The company expected to hit 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit by the end of this year, but Blue Origin’s New Glenn, one of its main launch vehicles, is out of service. candidates.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
candidates.raw_excerpt: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece. That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target. What's happening and when to look The Andromeda galaxy is at its most dramatic in photographs, not an eyepiece.
